items.title: Hg toolkit slim triangles products and four point constants
items.statement: Use unit-edge geometric realizations for Cayley graphs. A triangle is δ-slim if each side lies in the closed δ-neighbourhood of the other two. Set (x|y)_o=(d(o,x)+d(o,y)−d(x,y))/2. Product constant k means (x|z)_o≥min((x|y)_o,(y|z)_o)−k for every basepoint; four-point constant k means the largest two opposite-pair distance sums differ by at most 2k.
items.strategy: Declare δ,k≥0, allow degenerate triangles, and distinguish vertex word metric from the geodesic realization. This supplies vocabulary earlier than the published hyperbolicity definitions. Nonnegativity follows directly from 0=d(x,x)<=2d(x,y). Products are nonnegative by the triangle inequality and at most either radial distance. Neighbourhoods here mean point-to-set infimum <= radius; for compact sides the required attainment is proved locally using the closed interval parameter and bisection, not assumed for arbitrary closed sets.

references.title: Druţu–Kapovich Chapter 9 §§9.1,9.5

items.title: Hg toolkit local geodesics and hausdorff control
items.statement: A k-local geodesic is an arc-length path whose subpaths of length at most k are geodesic. Quasi-geodesics are maps of real intervals satisfying λ^−1|s−t|−ε≤d(q(s),q(t))≤λ|s−t|+ε. Hausdorff distance is the maximum of the two point-to-set suprema, with infima used for distances to sets. Hausdorff distance is used for nonempty images, takes values in [0,+infinity], and is not asserted to be a finite-valued metric on all subsets.
items.strategy: No continuity or properness is built into the quasi-geodesic definition. Any argument using polygonal interpolation must prove its constants separately. Distances to nonempty sets exist as infima of nonnegative real distances by the complete ordered-field property; unbounded suprema are +infinity. Compact intervals are nonempty, including one-point intervals.

references.title: Druţu–Kapovich Theorem 9.38 and §9.6

items.title: Hg toolkit hyperbolic group and stable length
items.statement: Fix a finite generating set S and a δ-slim geometric Cayley graph. This is the standing hyperbolic-group hypothesis. Define τ_S(g)=lim_n |g^n|_S/n once existence is proved. A group is elementary when finite or virtually cyclic.
items.strategy: Do not use independence of generating set as a prerequisite. Prove stable-length existence inline using subadditivity and division by a fixed integer. All later counting statements use finiteness of S. Write a_n=|g^n| and a_0=0. The power law and length subadditivity give a_(n+m)<=a_n+a_m. Put t=inf_(k>=1) a_k/k. For each fixed k, n=qk+r with 0<=r<k gives a_n/n<=q a_k/n+max_(r<k)a_r/n, hence limsup a_n/n<=a_k/k. Taking the infimum gives convergence to t; the lower bound t is immediate. This is the full Fekete argument, not a later theorem. The group definition assumes a specified geodesic unit-edge Cayley realization; the finite endpoint-candidate minimum supplies that realization and its vertex metric, using shortest words and partial endpoint edges.

references.title: Hamann §5.1 definitions and Proposition 5.2.5

items.title: Geodesic triangles in trees are tripods
items.statement: In the unit-edge realization of a connected graph with no cycles, unique geodesics between three points form a tripod, allowing legs of length zero.
items.strategy: Subdivide at the three points and common branchpoint. Two distinct simple paths would form a cycle. Supply the finite path-union argument even if the tree is infinite. A connected graph here has finite edge paths between vertices even when its vertex set is infinite. Delete loops from such a path; distinct simple paths enclose a finite cycle. For edge-interior endpoints subdivide finitely many edges, preserving this argument. The intersection of two paths from a common vertex is an initial finite path with a last point, and the remaining legs concatenate to the third path. Their edge lengths add, which proves the metric tripod claim.

references.title: Druţu–Kapovich §9.2 metric trees

items.title: Slim triangles imply the gromov product inequality
items.statement: In a geodesic space with δ-slim triangles, the product inequality holds with constant 3δ, for every basepoint.
items.strategy: Let α=min((x|y)_o,(y|z)_o). If α≤δ, nonnegativity suffices. Otherwise take 0≤t<α−δ and points at radius t on [o,x],[o,y],[o,z]. Every point of [x,y] has distance at least (x|y)_o from o, by triangle inequalities. Slimness therefore brings the radius-t point on [o,x] within δ of [o,y], and within 2δ of its radius-t point; repeat for y,z. The two outer points are within 4δ. Joining x,z through them gives (x|z)_o≥t−2δ. Let t increase to α−δ. This also covers δ=0 by the same limiting inequality. This elementary proof avoids the sign-corrupted manuscript extraction.

references.title: Druţu–Kapovich Lemmas 9.25 and 9.31

items.title: The gromov product inequality implies the four point condition
items.statement: The product inequality with constant k at every basepoint is equivalent, in any metric space, to the four-point inequality with largest-two-sum gap at most 2k.
items.strategy: Multiply by two, expand products, and cancel the distances from the basepoint. To recover the converse, designate each of the four points as basepoint. Geodesicity is unnecessary for this algebraic conversion.

references.title: Druţu–Kapovich §9.5 Gromov hyperbolicity

items.title: The four point condition implies slim triangles
items.statement: For a geodesic space satisfying the four-point condition with constant k, every geodesic triangle is 4k-slim.
items.strategy: For p on [a,b], set t=d(a,p) and α=(b|c)_a. If t≤α choose q on [a,c] at distance t from a; two product inequalities give (p|q)_a≥t−2k and hence d(p,q)≤4k. If t≥α use b and [b,c].

references.title: Druţu–Kapovich Lemma 9.32; conservative two-inequality constant

items.title: Halfspace separation for the local-geodesic mesh
items.statement: In a delta-slim geodesic space, delta>0, let x0,x1,x2 lie in this order on a geodesic with successive distances 3delta. Write D(a,b)={z:d(z,a)<=d(z,b)}. Then dist(D(x0,x1),D(x2,x1))>=delta, D(x2,x1) is contained in the strict complement of D(x0,x1), and dist(x0,D(x1,x0))>=3delta/2 (likewise at x2).
items.strategy: Take y0 in D(x0,x1), y2 in D(x2,x1), eta=d(y0,y2), and midpoint u on a geodesic between them. Put D_i=d(x_i,y_i) for i=0,2. Then d(u,x0)<=D_0+eta/2, d(u,x2)<=D_2+eta/2, and d(u,x1)>=max(D_0,D_2)-eta/2. Slimness in (x0,u,x2) supplies v within delta of x1 on one side, say [x0,u]. Then d(u,v)>=D_0-eta/2-delta, hence d(x0,v)<=eta+delta; therefore 3delta=d(x0,x1)<=eta+2delta. Use delta+e approximate witnesses and let e decrease to zero if attainment has not yet been established. Thus eta>=delta. The sets are disjoint since delta>0, proving strict nesting. For y in D(x1,x0), 3delta<=d(x0,y)+d(y,x1)<=2d(x0,y), proving the endpoint bound without choosing a closest bisector point. This removes the unnecessary nearest-bisector assumption in the source.

references.title: Drutu–Kapovich, revised Lemma 11.46, printed pp.375–377 (PDF indices 395–397)

items.title: Local geodesics in a hyperbolic space are uniform quasi geodesics
items.statement: If δ>0, every 6δ-local arc-length geodesic in a geodesic δ-slim space is a (3,4δ)-quasi-geodesic in the stated real-interval convention; hence the same holds for every k-local geodesic with k≥6δ. If δ=0, every k-local geodesic with k>0 is a global geodesic.
items.strategy: For delta>0 use the preceding halfspace lemma on the 3delta mesh of each compact subarc. Let H_i=D(x_(i+1),x_i), B_i its bisector. The lemma gives H_(i+1) contained in the interior of H_i and distance(B_i,B_(i+1))>=delta. Endpoint distances to the first/last bisectors are at least 3delta/2. Along a connecting geodesic, continuous distance differences vanish at successive first crossings of these nested sets, in increasing order. For n>=2 mesh pieces the distance is at least 3delta+(n-1)delta>=n delta; for n=0,1 use locality directly. A final remainder sigma<3delta gives d>=n delta-sigma=length/3-4sigma/3>=length/3-4delta. Arc length gives the upper inequality. For delta=0 first prove unique geodesics by applying zero slimness to degenerate triangles; closedness of compact segments follows directly from their isometric interval parameters. Initial segment intersections then give tripods. On a compact interval choose a finite subdivision with two adjacent lengths less than k. Inductively concatenate: the tripod of the old starting point, joining point and new endpoint can fail to be a single geodesic only by backtracking along a positive segment near the joining point, contradicting k-locality. Thus the whole path is geodesic. This uses positive k, never k=0.

references.title: Druţu–Kapovich, revised Theorem 11.45 and Lemma 11.46, pp.375–378

items.title: Hg toolkit polygonal interpolation of quasi geodesics
items.statement: If a (λ,ε)-quasi-geodesic map of a nonempty compact real interval has endpoints at distance at least 2ε, there is a continuous (λ,4ε)-quasi-geodesic with the same endpoints that is 2λ-Lipschitz, is pointwise within 4ε, and whose image is at Hausdorff distance at most 2ε from the original image. If the endpoint distance is less than 2ε, the original image lies within 3λ²ε+ε of its initial endpoint.
items.strategy: Reproduce the complete AFP interpolation proof. For ε=0 use the original map. For ε>0, mark parameter points at gaps ε/λ, with the last two gaps in [ε/λ,3ε/(2λ)], and join successive image points by constant-speed geodesics. Prove the 2λ Lipschitz bound interval by interval; prove the upper quasi-geodesic inequality by splitting at marked points; prove the lower inequality by the same-interval, adjacent-interval and separated-interval cases, using the 2/5 split in the last case to obtain additive error 4ε. The nearest marked point gives pointwise distance 4ε and both Hausdorff inclusions with bound 2ε. Handle the short endpoint case separately: the lower quasi-geodesic inequality bounds the parameter interval by 3λε and the upper inequality bounds every image point from the initial endpoint by 3λ²ε+ε. These cases cover discontinuous maps and retain the endpoint hypothesis omitted in older formulations.

references.title: Gouëzel–Shchur, corrected quantitative Morse lemma, Lemma 2.1
Gouëzel, AFP Gromov_Hyperbolicity, Isometries.thy, quasi_geodesic_made_lipschitz

items.title: Exponential contraction of projection away from a quasiconvex set
items.statement: Let a geodesic space have product-hyperbolicity constant κ≥0 and let ρ>κ. Here Y is K-quasiconvex if every two points of Y admit a geodesic contained in its closed K-neighbourhood. Let supplied closest points p_a,p_b project the endpoints of a (λ,ε)-quasi-geodesic map [a,b] to a K-quasiconvex set Y. If the whole image stays distance at least D from Y and D≥15ρ/2+K+ε/2, then d(p_a,p_b) is at most 2K+8ρ plus the maximum of 5κ and 4√2λ(b−a)exp(−(D−K−ε/2)log(2)/(5ρ)). No existence of closest points to an arbitrary nonproper quasiconvex set is asserted.
items.strategy: Reproduce the corrected projection proof from Gouëzel–Shchur Lemmas 2.4–2.5 and the AFP theory. Work with ρ>κ. First prove the basic closest-point inequality for the supplied endpoint projections to a K-quasiconvex target. Subdivide the parameter interval into 2^N pieces whose images are at most 10ρ+ε apart, move the subdivision points 5ρ toward the target, discard alternate points, and induct for k=floor((D−K−ε/2−15ρ/2)/(5ρ)) stages. Treat separately the short interval and block-decomposition cases and sum the surviving projection gaps; the ceiling/floor inequalities give the displayed exponential term. For a geodesic segment, compactness supplies closest points; in the nested-neighborhood application construct the projections explicitly along the compact base segment. This is the corrected decreasing-sequence estimate; do not use the reversed integral inequality from the superseded 2013 proof. A later limit ρ↓κ removes the strict auxiliary inequality; the κ=0 Morse case is handled without dividing by κ.

references.title: Gouëzel–Shchur, corrected quantitative Morse lemma, Lemmas 2.4–2.5
Gouëzel, AFP Morse_Gromov_Theorem.thy, complete projection contraction proof

items.title: Morse stability with explicit parameter dependence
items.statement: Assume AC for the following projection-family proof. For λ≥1, ε≥0 and δ≥0, the image of every possibly discontinuous (λ,ε)-quasi-geodesic map of a compact real interval into a geodesic δ-slim space has Hausdorff distance at most M=92λ²(ε+3δ) from every geodesic with the same endpoints.
items.strategy: Use the earlier slim-to-product lemma, so the product-hyperbolicity constant is κ=3δ, and reproduce the corrected Gouëzel–Shchur/AFP proof locally. For endpoint distance at least 2ε, use the preceding interpolation lemma to obtain a continuous 2λ-Lipschitz (λ,C)-quasi-geodesic with C=4ε and image Hausdorff distance at most 2ε; for the complementary case use the direct 3λ²ε+ε bound. For the continuous path, prove the projection small-gap lemma and the preceding exponential contraction estimate. With an auxiliary constant κ'>κ, set L=18κ', D=55κ' and α=12/100. Induct on interval length in steps κ'/(4λ): at a point z, project to the comparison geodesic; if the Gromov product is at most L, stop; if both side minima are at most D+4C, apply the quasi-geodesic inequalities directly; otherwise use the nested neighborhoods V_j of the projection segment and the exponential estimate. Split its gain into α and 1−α, obtaining the telescoping exponential recurrence and the one-sided bound λ²(11C/2+91κ'). Let κ' decrease to κ. For the reverse Hausdorff inclusion, cover the connected interpolated image by the two closed thickenings of the comparison-geodesic subsegments on either side of a chosen point; their intersection and slimness give one extra κ, hence λ²(11C/2+92κ). Finally add the original/interpolated image error 2ε: since C=4ε and λ≥1, the ε coefficient is at most 22λ²+2≤24λ²≤92λ², yielding 92λ²(ε+κ). This covers arbitrary, possibly discontinuous compact-interval maps and proves both inclusions. The κ=ε=0 case follows directly from the tripod argument, with no division by zero. The paper is an exposition; the exact 92-constant inequalities are to be copied from and checked against the complete AFP proof, not cited as an external dependency. Explicit AC use: select the family of geodesic segments joining f(t) to its chosen projection as t varies over the compact parameter interval in the nested-neighbourhood construction. Projections to a fixed parametrized compact segment can instead use their least minimizing parameter; finite interpolation choices do not themselves need AC. Keep the elementary zero-constant branch choice-free.

references.title: Gouëzel–Shchur, Theorem 1.1 and corrected proof architecture
Gouëzel, AFP Morse_Gromov_Theorem.thy, complete exact-constant proof

items.title: A quasi isometry of geodesic spaces has a controlled coarse inverse
items.statement: Assume AC. For a (lambda,epsilon)-quasi-isometric embedding f:X->Y with the attained coarse-density bound R, there is g:Y->X with d(fg(y),y)<=R and d(gf(x),x)<=lambda(R+epsilon), and g is a (lambda,lambda(2R+epsilon))-quasi-isometric embedding. If a selector g is supplied, these estimates are choice-free.
items.strategy: Read and specialize the earlier quasi-inverse theorem: AC selects one x from {x:d(f(x),y)<=R} for every y. Upper bound d(g(y),g(z))<=lambda(d(y,z)+2R+epsilon); lower bound >=(d(y,z)-2R-epsilon)/lambda. The common additive constant lambda(2R+epsilon) dominates both. Set y=f(x) for the second composite estimate. No geodesicity is used in the estimate. Supplied g requires no choice.

references.title: Druţu–Kapovich Corollary 9.39; local published coarse-inverse theorem

items.title: Hyperbolicity is transported by a quasi isometry
items.statement: Assume AC for the Morse supplier. If f:X→Y is a (λ,ε)-quasi-isometric embedding of geodesic spaces and Y is δ-slim, then X is λ(2M(λ,ε,δ)+δ+ε)-slim. Hence quasi-isometric geodesic spaces share hyperbolicity.
items.strategy: Map a geodesic triangle into Y, replace its three quasi-geodesic sides by geodesics using both locally proved Hausdorff inclusions, use slimness in Y, and apply the lower inequality for f. Substituting the preceding explicit M proves the displayed constant; no unresolved Morse function or external theorem remains in this proof contract.

references.title: Druţu–Kapovich Corollary 9.39

items.title: Short loop relators give a finite dehn presentation
items.statement: After replacing δ by an integer Δ≥3 with Δ≥2δ, take all null words of length at most 10Δ as relators. This finite set presents G and admits strict Dehn shortening for every nonempty freely reduced null word, with cyclic and based formulations distinguished.
items.strategy: Use a positive hyperbolicity upper bound, including for trees, and integer Delta>=max(3,2*delta). If every based subword of length <=5*Delta is geodesic, bracket each real subarc of length <=6*delta by vertices; the bracketing adds at most two, and 6*delta+2<=5*Delta. The entire path is 6*delta-local, so its (3,4*delta) bound at equal endpoints forces length<=12*delta. This contradicts length>10*Delta. Thus a based nongeodesic subword of length<=5*Delta has a strictly shorter geodesic replacement and gives a relator of length<10*Delta containing the subword as more than half its length. Null words of length<=10*Delta are relators themselves. Strict length descent proves presentation and the based Dehn algorithm; the same yields the cyclic version. Use the reduced-word universal property to obtain the surjection F(S)->G. Each Dehn replacement changes a word by a conjugate of a relator, so induction on length proves kernel containment in the normal closure and the reverse containment holds since every chosen relator is null. Include formal inverse symbols even if different letters evaluate to the same element. Finite words of length at most 10Delta over a finite alphabet form a finite set.

references.title: Druţu–Kapovich §9.13, Theorem 9.108, Proposition 9.109 and Lemma 9.112 pp.246–249

items.title: Linear isoperimetry implies uniformly thin geodesic bigons
items.statement: Assuming the Axiom of Choice, for a finite presentation with maximum relator length L and Area(w)≤K|w| for every null word, the geometric Cayley graph has uniformly slim geodesic triangles, with a constant depending only on K and L; consequently its geodesic bigons are uniformly thin.
items.strategy: Assume AC and invoke the two earlier, proved HG-P supplier results with this finite presentation, area constant K and maximum relator perimeter L. Verify their filling conventions and retain their endpoint discretization errors. The uniformity lemma, not qualitative hyperbolicity alone, supplies dependence only on K,L. A geodesic bigon is a degenerate triangle, giving the final claim. Do not author this consumer before both named HG-P items are published; its former unsupported cone extraction is removed.

references.title: Druţu–Kapovich, revised Proposition 9.104, Proposition 11.176 and Theorem 11.181

items.title: Infinite order elements have positive stable translation length
items.statement: For every infinite-order element g of a finitely generated hyperbolic group, n↦g^n is a quasi-isometric embedding and τ_S(g)>0.
items.strategy: Use Hamann 5.2.5 midpoint counting with n0=|B_(4δ+1)(1)| to prove linear lower growth, then divide by n and use the subadditive limit. Spell out graph integer rounding and the midpoint-neighbourhood count. This is for the Cayley action, not arbitrary hyperbolic-space isometries.

references.title: Hamann Proposition 5.2.5 pp.87–89, complete proof read

items.title: Axis fellow travelling controls the centralizer
items.statement: For an infinite-order element g in a finitely generated hyperbolic group, C_G(g)/<g> has finitely many cosets. More precisely each coset meets a ball of radius depending on δ and the quasi-geodesic constants of the power orbit. Here C_G(g)={h in G: hg=gh}; the index means the number of cosets of the cyclic subgroup.
items.strategy: Use the quadrilateral with vertices 1,g^m,hg^m,h and choose m so its long midpoint avoids the short sides. Morse gives indices i,j with |hg^(j−i)|≤2M+2δ plus graph rounding. Count the finite ball. No torsion-abelian-subgroup result is used.

references.title: Hamann Theorem 5.2.6 pp.89–90, complete proof read

items.title: Hg toolkit gromov sequences and boundary product
items.statement: A sequence (x_n) is Gromov if (x_n|x_m)_o→∞ as n,m→∞. Two such sequences are asymptotic if the mixed products diverge jointly. Define the boundary as equivalence classes once proved, and define (ξ|η)_o as the supremum over representing sequences of liminf_(n,m) (x_n|y_m)_o. For a double sequence a_nm>=0, liminf_(n,m) means sup_N inf_{n,m>=N} a_nm, with +infinity allowed. The class-labelled supremum is introduced only after the following equivalence proof; before it one works with representing sequences.
items.strategy: Do not use a one-index diagonal limit as the definition. Introduce the quotient only after the equivalence proof; give extended-real conventions. Product neighbourhoods and their topology require a separate well-definedness argument.

references.title: Druţu–Kapovich §9.9 ray-boundary treatment; sequence comparison expanded locally

items.title: Asymptotic gromov sequences form an equivalence relation
items.statement: Mixed-product divergence is an equivalence relation on Gromov sequences, and the relation is unchanged by changing the basepoint.
items.strategy: Reflexivity is the Gromov condition and symmetry is immediate. For transitivity insert one sufficiently far point of the middle sequence in the product inequality. Changing basepoint changes finite products by at most d(o,o′).

references.title: Druţu–Kapovich §9.5 product inequality; §9.9 boundary conventions

items.title: Boundary products are independent of representative and basepoint
items.statement: Boundary-product values from different representatives agree up to an additive bound depending on the product hyperbolicity constant, and moving o to o′ changes the extended product by at most d(o,o′). Product neighbourhoods define a Hausdorff topology independent of these choices.
items.strategy: Let κ be the product constant. Applying the product inequality twice to representatives x,x' of ξ and y,y' of η shows that any mixed liminf differs from the supremal boundary product by at most 2κ; changing basepoint changes every product by at most d(o,o'). Define U_R(ξ)={η:(ξ|η)_o>R}. The same inequality, with thresholds shifted by 2κ, gives refinement and intersection axioms; distinct classes have finite product, which gives disjoint threshold neighbourhoods. This proves Hausdorffness and representative/basepoint independence. For a proper space, the next lemma identifies these neighbourhoods with the ray-boundary ones. For full precision use a conservative extended triangle constant 3kappa: two representative changes cost at most 2kappa and the finite product inequality costs kappa. U_R need not itself be open. Declare O open exactly when each xi in O has some U_R(xi) contained in O; the shifted triangle inequality proves the neighbourhood refinement axioms and that U_(R+3kappa+1)(xi) is contained in the interior of U_R(xi). If xi!=eta, choose R>(xi|eta)+3kappa; U_R(xi) and U_R(eta) are disjoint. Use their interiors for Hausdorff separation. Changing representatives/basepoints shifts thresholds only. Infinite product means mixed divergence, hence equality of classes; handle this separately rather than subtract infinities.

references.title: Druţu–Kapovich §9.9, ray topology; sequence-product comparison requires additional full treatment

items.title: Hg toolkit proper ray compactness and sequence comparison
items.statement: Assume AC for the simultaneous representative/geodesic selections and diagonal subsequences. For a proper geodesic hyperbolic space, each Gromov-sequence class has a geodesic ray representative from a fixed basepoint. The ray quotient topology agrees with the product topology, and the boundary is compact.
items.strategy: Choose representatives with products tending to infinity and geodesic segments from the basepoint. Properness makes each closed integer-radius ball compact; successively extract subsequences converging on every integer ball and diagonalize. The 1-Lipschitz parametrizations converge uniformly on compact intervals to a geodesic ray. Slim triangles and product inequalities show the ray's integer sequence is equivalent to the original Gromov sequence. The representative comparison bound from the preceding lemma identifies product and fellow-travelling neighbourhoods. Repeating the diagonal argument for arbitrary boundary sequences gives sequential compactness; the countable product-neighbourhood basis is metrizable, hence compactness.

references.title: Druţu–Kapovich Lemma 9.61, Corollary 9.62 and Lemma 9.66; full comparison still to be sourced

items.title: Quasi isometries extend to boundary homeomorphisms
items.statement: Assume AC for the Morse/coarse-inverse proof. A quasi-isometry between geodesic hyperbolic spaces induces a homeomorphism of their Gromov-sequence boundaries; bounded-distance maps induce the same map and extensions respect composition. Properness is needed for the compact ray-boundary package, not imposed on this sequence statement.
items.strategy: If two sequences have mixed product tending to infinity, their geodesics from the basepoint share longer initial portions up to the product constant. Images of those portions are uniform quasi-geodesics; Morse stability makes endpoint geodesics in the target share initial portions whose lengths tend to infinity. Thus a quasi-isometry sends Gromov sequences and equivalent representatives to well-defined target classes. The same threshold estimate proves continuity in the product topology. Bounded-distance maps give equivalent image sequences, composition is pointwise, and a controlled coarse inverse supplies the inverse boundary map. This argument does not use properness; the proper-ray lemma is needed only for the compact ray model.

references.title: Druţu–Kapovich Theorem 9.83 (proper ray case); full proof and nonproper adaptation still required

items.title: Hg toolkit loxodromics and independent poles
items.statement: An isometry is loxodromic when its integer orbit is a quasi-isometric embedding of Z. Its two boundary limits are its poles. Two loxodromics are independent when their two pole sets are disjoint.
items.strategy: Prove existence and distinctness of the two poles using orbit quasi-geodesicity and Morse, before using the terminology. In the finitely generated hyperbolic group case every infinite-order element is loxodromic by the earlier lemma.

references.title: Hamann §5.3 after Proposition 5.2.5

items.title: Hg toolkit finitely many cayley cone types
items.statement: For a finite generating set of a hyperbolic group, only finitely many geodesic cone types occur; a cone at g records all h for which |gh|=|g|+|h|.
items.strategy: Use the standard finite-cone-type proof in a δ-hyperbolic Cayley graph. The values |gv|−|g| for |v|≤2δ+1 determine whether a geodesic word from 1 to g can be extended by any word: thin quadrilaterals reduce the first possible failure of additivity to that ball. These values are integers in a finite interval, and the ball is finite, so only finitely many patterns and hence cone types occur. Include the first-failure induction rather than cite finite generation alone.

references.title: Hamann Proposition 5.2.3 pp.85–87; complete proof

items.title: Hg toolkit infinite hyperbolic groups have infinite order elements
items.statement: Every infinite finitely generated hyperbolic group has an element of infinite order.
items.strategy: Local finiteness and infinitude give an infinite geodesic ray by the finite-branching path lemma. Two vertices g_i,g_j on it, i<j, have the same cone type. If u labels the intervening nonempty segment, equality of cones implies inductively that u can be appended after every translated copy while preserving length additivity. Hence |g_i u^n|=i+n(j−i), so u represents an infinite-order element. Avoid an undeclared general Konig lemma: order the finite alphabet once, form the tree of geodesic words from the identity, and recursively choose its first child that has extensions of arbitrarily large length. Finite branching ensures one exists at each stage. This deterministic recursion is choice-free. The cone repetition induction then applies.

references.title: Hamann Proposition 5.2.2 and Theorem 5.2.4 pp.85–87; complete proofs

items.title: Hg toolkit non elementary groups have independent loxodromics
items.statement: A finitely generated hyperbolic group that is neither finite nor virtually cyclic contains two infinite-order elements with disjoint pole sets.
items.strategy: Follow Hamann Theorems 5.3.7–5.3.8. The preceding lemma supplies an infinite-order g and its quasi-axis R. If the boundary had two points, every translate of a geodesic double ray with those endpoints stays uniformly close to R; vertex transitivity makes R cobounded, so the group has two ends and is virtually cyclic. Thus a non-elementary group has infinite boundary. Choose f with d(f,R)>2δ and put h=fgf^-1. The pole union of g and h has at least three points. Hamann's argument rules out exactly three: a shared pole gives arbitrarily long paired subsegments of the equivariant quasi-axes, and equivariance propagates the bounded-distance pairing in both directions, forcing both poles to agree. Hence the union has four points and g,h are independent. No torsion-free corollary or later free-subgroup theorem is used. Required local repairs before using this route: if the whole group is uniformly close to the power orbit <g>, a finite ball meets every coset, so <g> has finite index; this avoids importing the two-ends classification. To rule out one shared pole, select infinitely many distinct pairs (i,j) along the common half-axis with bounded d(g^i,h^j). Finiteness of the ball gives two pairs with the SAME element g^(-i)h^j, not merely distances bounded by the same number. Their equality implies g^(i2-i1)=h^(j2-j1); choose pairs with both differences nonzero. Equal nonzero powers have the same two poles. A claim that bounded distances alone propagate for all integer translates is not a proof. The ideal-line existence and uniform orbit/line comparison must still be supplied by the preceding boundary/Morse machinery.

references.title: Hamann Theorems 5.3.7–5.3.8 pp.91–94; complete torsion-allowed proof

items.title: Independent loxodromics have disjoint pole neighbourhoods
items.statement: Independent loxodromics have four pairwise disjoint pole neighbourhoods in the boundary.
items.strategy: Separate four distinct points by the Hausdorff topology and refine finitely many neighbourhoods. This does not prove that a non-elementary hyperbolic group possesses independent elements; that extra supplier is required for the published rank-two-free-subgroup consumer.

references.title: Canary Theorem 7.3 pp.32–33; four-pole separation

items.title: Loxodromic elements have north south boundary dynamics
items.statement: Assume AC for the compactness/selection proof. For an infinite-order element g of a finitely generated hyperbolic group and neighbourhoods U± of its poles, there is N such that g^n(∂G minus U−)⊂U+ and g^−n(∂G minus U+)⊂U− for all n≥N.
items.strategy: For a non-elementary group use Canary Theorem 5.7, whose proof shows that every divergent sequence has a subsequence converging uniformly on compact subsets away from one repelling point. Apply it to any subsequence of g^n. Proposition 5.1 identifies the only possible attractor and repeller as g+ and g−, so every subsequence has a further subsequence with the same uniform limit; a contradiction argument gives uniform convergence of the whole sequence on the compact set ∂G\U−. This is exactly the stated neighbourhood inclusion. Apply the same argument to g^-1. In the elementary infinite case the boundary is the two-point pole set, so the inclusion is immediate.

references.title: Canary Proposition 5.1 pp.25–26 and Theorem 5.7 pp.28–29; complete convergence-action proof

items.title: Free Cayley trees from reduced-word normal form
items.statement: The unit-edge Cayley realization of the reduced-word free group on a finite alphabet is a geodesic tree. A reduced edge path is globally geodesic, including all real subintervals.
items.strategy: In the reduced-word model every vertex is reached from the empty word by its letters. For an oriented edge v->w=vs its label is v^(-1)w=s. Along a simple cycle the ordered product of these labels telescopes to the identity. Adjacent inverse labels would immediately repeat a vertex, so a cycle would give a nonempty reduced identity word, contradicting the proved reduced-word normal form. Hence the graph is acyclic and connected. Unique simple paths and finite subdivision at interior points are supplied by the earlier tripod lemma. A reduced path cannot repeat a vertex, since the intervening nonempty word would then be a reduced identity; thus it is the unique simple path between its endpoints. The induced edge-length distance is its length, and replacing a subarc by a shorter path would contradict this minimality.

references.title: Reduced-word construction: local adaptation of the earlier proved free-group item; Drutu–Kapovich metric tree discussion

items.title: Quantitative hyperbolic geometry toolkit
items.statement: Package the preceding equivalences, local-to-global and Morse bounds, quasi-isometry invariance, finite Dehn presentation and filling converse, stable length, centralizers and boundary functoriality/dynamics, with each clause retaining its own hypotheses and constants. State AC on the filling, selected inverse, Morse projection-family and boundary compactness clauses of this proof; retain the elementary metric equivalences and supplied-selector estimates choice-free.
items.strategy: Conjoin the preceding results without strengthening their hypotheses. Substitute the explicit local-to-global constants and M=92λ²(ε+3δ); state the filling converse as slim triangles; distinguish the sequence boundary from its proper compact ray model; and invoke the independent-loxodromic and uniform north–south lemmas before ping-pong. Each clause is already in dependency order, so the package is a bookkeeping proof rather than a new geometric argument.

references.title: Druţu–Kapovich Chapter 9; Hamann §§5.1–5.3; Canary §§5,7

items.title: Morse stability in a tree
items.statement: A geodesic segment in a tree is its unique endpoint geodesic and has Hausdorff distance zero from it. A path that goes distance a out a branch and returns has a repeated point separated by parameter length 2a, so (λ,ε)-quasi-geodesicity forces a≤λε/2.
items.strategy: Verify the zero case and apply the lower quasi-geodesic inequality to the two visits to the branchpoint. This is a sharp obstruction to arbitrary backtracking, not a proof of general Morse stability.

references.title: Druţu–Kapovich §9.2 and Theorem 9.38; tree specialization

items.title: A local geodesic constant in a cayley graph
items.statement: In the unit-edge Cayley tree of a free group, a reduced edge path is geodesic on every subinterval and hence is (1,0)-quasi-geodesic globally.
items.strategy: Apply the earlier locally proved free Cayley-tree normal form and unique path argument. Every reduced edge path and its real subintervals are geodesic. At delta=0 use any positive locality radius k, as required by the earlier local-geodesic lemma.

references.title: Druţu–Kapovich §9.2, free-tree specialization

items.title: Boundary extension of a tree quasi isometry
items.statement: Left translation by a free-group element acts isometrically on its Cayley tree and extends to its end boundary by concatenation followed by cancellation of a finite prefix.
items.strategy: Use infinite reduced rays and verify a bound on prefix cancellation by the translating word length; cylinder neighbourhoods prove continuity and the inverse translation gives the inverse. Prove the tree case directly: two root rays share a finite prefix of length equal to their product; a Gromov sequence has arbitrarily long compatible prefixes and determines a unique infinite reduced word. Conversely its prefix sequence is Gromov. Concatenation with a translating word cancels at most its length, so a cylinder of prefix length n+|g| maps into the appropriate cylinder of length n. Left invariance gives the isometry and the inverse word gives the inverse boundary map. This directly proves the stated specialization without assuming the general boundary-extension theorem.

references.title: Hamann §5.3, tree specialization

items.title: Ping pong for two loxodromics
items.statement: If independent loxodromics satisfy the four uniform pole-neighbourhood inclusions, sufficiently large positive powers generate a rank-two free subgroup.
items.strategy: Give the reduced-word ping-pong proof, including cyclic conjugation of a reduced word when its first and last letters require it. Do not replace uniform neighbourhood inclusions by pointwise convergence.

references.title: Canary Theorem 7.3 pp.32–33

items.title: Properness is needed for the compact boundary package
items.statement: The metric tree obtained by attaching countably infinitely many copies of [0,∞) at their zero endpoints is geodesic and 0-hyperbolic, is not proper, and has a countably infinite discrete noncompact Gromov boundary.
items.strategy: Points at distance one on distinct rays are pairwise distance two, so the closed unit ball is not compact. Distinct ends have product zero, so positive product neighbourhoods are singletons; the singleton open cover has no finite subcover. A Gromov sequence must eventually lie on a single ray: joint products greater than one exclude points on different rays; within that ray its radii tend to infinity. Thus there are exactly the stated countably many classes, with no extra non-ray classes. The unit sphere points form a pairwise 2-separated set, and the radius-less-than-one cover of the unit ball has no finite subcover.

references.title: Druţu–Kapovich Corollary 9.62, explicit failure without properness
